title: The Many Senses of Visual Similarity: A Text-Prompted Image Perceptual Metric

paper.title: The Many Senses of Visual Similarity: A Text-Prompted Image Perceptual Metric
paper.abstract:
Abstract Human visual similarity judgments are context-dependent. For example, two images may be similar in shape but distinct in color. Existing perceptual similarity metrics, however, collapse these nuances into a single scalar value, offering no mechanism to condition on specific aspects. To bridge this gap, we introduce a large-scale dataset of human similarity judgments over image triplets, where each triplet is annotated across multiple, free-form semantic aspects of similarity. Benchmarking a broad range of frontier vision-language models (VLMs) reveals a considerable performance gap compared to human annotators’ concensus. Leveraging our data, we fine-tune a VLM to produce our Text-Prompted Image Perceptual Similarity (TPIPS) metric, capturing multiple senses of visual similarity depending on the specified text prompt.
We demonstrate that TPIPS aligns more closely with human perception and generalizes reliably beyond the training distribution. Finally, we show that TPIPS unlocks new capabilities in text-guided retrieval, compositional search, and the fine-grained evaluation of generative models. Our code, data, and trained models are at https://peterwang512.github.io/TPIPS .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Figure 1 : The Many Senses of Similarity. Given a reference image (top left), the four candidate images (top right) are similar to the reference in different ways, such as subject color, pose, ground surface, or texture. But existing visual similarity measures (L2, SSIM [ 1 ] , LPIPS [ 2 ] , Dreamsim [ 3 ] ) collapse similarity into a single scalar, and thus producing ambiguous and inconsistent results. Our Text-Prompted Image Perceptual Similarity (TPIPS) can be conditioned on a particular sense of similarity (aspect), prompt-able by free-form text. With conditioning, this visual similarity problem is no longer ambiguous, and our method selects the most similar image aligned with human perceptual judgements. A long line of psychology research has established that human similarity judgments are context-dependent [ 4 , 5 ] . The same holds for images: there are many senses of visual similarity, depending on which aspect (color, texture, illumination, semantics, style, etc) is being compared. Consider Figure 1 : given the reference cow statue image (left), it is not immediately obvious which of the four candidate images on the right is the most similar overall to the reference. However, the answer becomes clear if the similarity judgement is conditioned on a specific visual aspect , such as the cow’s color, pose, or the image background. The image processing and computer vision communities have spent decades making progress on capturing human perceptual similarity, from hand-engineered distances like SSIM and others [ 1 , 6 , 7 ] to learned metrics trained on annotated human similarity judgments, such as LPIPS [ 2 ] or DreamSim [ 3 ] . These methods, however, model similarity as a single, scalar quantity, without conditioning on the aspect of the comparison. While previous methods add a notion of conditioning by leveraging vision-language models [ 8 , 9 , 10 ] , to our knowledge, no dataset collected with human perceptual similarity judgments exists to serve as validation. To fill this gap, we collect a large-scale dataset of one million human similarity judgments over 25K image triplets. Following triplet-based protocols standard in perceptual similarity studies [ 2 , 3 , 11 ] , annotators provide relative perceptual judgements by comparing three images and indicating which are most or least similar. Different from prior work, we extend this protocol to perceptual judgements conditioned on various visual aspects. We collect 260K triplet-aspect condition combinations, where each triplet is annotated conditioned on multiple free-form visual aspects, each aspect yielding a separate set of similarity judgments. The triplets are generated using text-to-image models and designed to be challenging. If the differences between candidates are too subtle, humans cannot reliably judge similarity; if they are too coarse, the task collapses to judging overall similarity, which current models already handle. We target the middle ground, with images that differ along multiple aspects simultaneously — through fine-grained variations in properties such as color, lighting, and texture. We use this syntheic dataset to construct a benchmark and evaluate a broad set of baselines, including recent open-source and proprietary VLMs [ 12 , 13 , 14 , 15 ] and state-of-the-art multimodal embedding models [ 16 , 17 ] , revealing room for improvement. We find that even the strongest current VLM systems often do not agree with human similarity judgments on specified aspects. We carefully propose and analyze different architecture choices for tuning a VLM into an aspect-conditioned perceptual metric on our collected perceptual data. Our model, Text-Prompted Image Perceptual Similarity (TPIPS), narrows the performance gap considerably. To assess whether our metric remains reliable beyond the synthetic training distribution, we collect a second set of human similarity judgments over outputs generated by external algorithms, designed for four different vision and graphics tasks, spanning both generative and non-generative pipelines. Our model outperforms baselines in this setting too, suggesting that it can serve as a general-purpose perceptual metric for aspect-conditioned evaluation. We show several downstream applications: evaluation of generative vision models, where output and reference similarity is measured along specified visual axes, nearest-neighbor retrieval, where the same query image returns different neighbors under different aspects, and compositional retrieval, where multiple query images, each conditioned on a different visual aspect, can be combined to find images that match the criteria. Our code, data, and trained models are at https://peterwang512.github.io/TPIPS .

sections.heading: 2 Related Works
sections.text: Perceptual similarity and preferences. Comparing two images is a fundamental problem in vision, with early approaches relying on hand-engineered, patch-based metrics [ 1 , 6 , 7 ] . With advances in deep image recognition [ 18 , 19 , 20 , 21 , 22 , 23 ] , learned deep features have been found to provide a more useful similarity signal than hand-engineered descriptors [ 2 , 24 , 25 , 26 , 27 ] . LPIPS [ 2 ] , PieAPP [ 28 ] , and DISTS [ 29 ] directly optimize deep features to align better with human judgments on low-level distortions. DreamSim [ 3 ] learns human perceptual judgments on synthesized images with high-level variations. Muttenthaler et al. [ 30 ] study perceptual judgments across object categories with THINGS [ 11 ] . Other works improve metric robustness to spatial shifts [ 31 ] , adversarial perturbations [ 32 ] , and arbitrary transformations [ 33 ] . Alternative metrics isolate specific attributes like style [ 34 , 35 ] or relationships between visual elements [ 36 ] . While these methods predict a single similarity score, similarity is inherently multi-faceted [ 4 ] . We address this by introducing a benchmark and model for human similarity judgements conditioned on various visual aspects. A separate but adjacent line of work uses pairwise human comparisons over generated or edited images to learn a scalar quality score over a single image [ 37 , 38 , 39 , 40 ] . In contrast, we learn from triplet judgments to model pairwise similarity conditioned on visual aspects. Conditional representation. Various research has studied learning representations of an input conditioned on different aspects. A line of work explores learning conditional representation given an explicit aspect, but assumes a fixed, finite vocabulary of conditions [ 41 , 42 , 43 , 44 , 45 ] . More recent work generalizes the condition input to free-form text, including training-free methods via vision-language models [ 46 , 47 , 48 ] and training-based methods that curate conditional supervision. GeneCIS [ 8 ] and FocalLens [ 9 ] mine attribute-difference triplets from existing vision-language datasets, while Omni-Attribute [ 10 ] bootstraps supervision from VLM-generated labels and TF-QARE [ 48 ] prompts for an image’s object, background, or style and averages the embedding of the resulting description. A parallel line of work studies context-conditional categorization [ 49 , 50 ] , and composed image retrieval [ 51 , 52 , 53 , 54 ] takes image-text inputs but uses the text to specify how the retrieved images should be different from the query image. Unlike prior conditional similarity work, we collect human similarity judgments directly under each aspect condition. This captures fine-grained relative differences not reliably present in image captions and VLM outputs, better aligning our method with human judgments than prior training-free, training-based methods and state-of-the-art VLMs. Vision-language models. Early vision-language models targeted a small number of tasks: dual-encoder contrastive models [ 22 , 55 , 56 ] such as CLIP [ 22 ] align image and text representations for retrieval and classification, while encoder-decoder models such as BLIP [ 57 , 58 ] added captioning and visual question answering. Modern instruction-tuned multimodal models including Qwen-VL series [ 59 , 60 , 14 , 61 ] and others [ 62 , 63 , 15 , 64 ] , and frontier proprietary systems such as Gemini [ 13 ] and GPT [ 12 ] —are trained on a much broader task mixtures [ 63 , 60 , 15 ] that, in some cases, also includes similarity benchmarks such as NIGHTS [ 3 ] and GeneCIS [ 8 ] . A parallel line of universal multimodal embedders, such as VLM2Vec [ 16 , 65 ] and Qwen3-VL-Embedding [ 17 ] , repurposes these backbones for instruction-conditioned retrieval. While VLMs can solve various vision tasks, we find that the performance gap remains for VLMs to yield human-aligned pairwise similarity judgments conditioned on specified aspects. Our benchmark and models aid in closing this gap.

sections.heading: 3 Dataset collection
sections.text: Our goal is to collect a dataset of similarity judgments 𝒟 \mathcal{D} , such that they can be used to train and evaluate a text-conditioned similarity algorithm. Human perceptual similarity is inherently relative: given a small set of candidates (e.g., 3 images), people can reliably identify the most different item, or the closer pair, with respect to visual aspects such as lighting, object pose, or background [ 4 ] . To do so, as shown in Figure 2 , we collect two datasets: (1) a large, synthetic dataset on odd-one-out judgments, which we use for training, and (2) a smaller set on other vision and graphics algorithms to validate the generalization of our algorithm on real-world applications.

sections.heading: 3.1 Odd-one-out dataset
sections.text: Given a pair of images, humans cannot reliably provide a similarity score directly, which led previous works to collect relative comparisons from image triplets by asking which of two image variations is closer to a given reference [ 2 , 3 ] , or which image is the most different [ 11 ] . In this setting, we adopt the odd-one-out task [ 11 ] , and extend it to perceptual judgements conditioned on various visual aspects. That is, given a triplet, 𝐗 = { 𝐱 1 , 𝐱 2 , 𝐱 3 } \mathbf{X}=\{\mathbf{x}_{1},\mathbf{x}_{2},\mathbf{x}_{3}\} , we ask annotators to the pick one that looks most different under the text guidance 𝐜 \mathbf{c} , recording it the result as y y . To construct our dataset, we curate a diverse yet controlled set of image variations. A core challenge lies in identifying an optimal difficulty regime: triplets must be neither trivial, where differences are too vast, nor uninformative, where differences are negligible. Furthermore, images within a single triplet must exhibit variation across multiple independent text-conditioned aspects to necessitate multi-faceted reasoning. Randomly sampling from large-scale image datasets or subsampling a video dataset typically yields degenerate triplets, where one image is an outlier across all aspects or the visual distance between the images is too great to allow for meaningful comparison. Inspired by Fu et al. [ 3 ] , we leverage text-to-image (T2I), language (LLM), and vision-language (VLM) models to propose candidate triplets and text conditionings at scale. We generate candidate triplets by sampling prompts from FLUX-Reason-6M [ 66 ] . A straightforward approach is to sample images from the same prompt, but this often fails to produce sufficiently diverse variations. As such, we use a language model to generate variations of a given prompt, before rendering the triplet. This produces a controlled yet diverse candidate set, while allowing humans to judge which of the text-induced variations are actually reflected in the images. Text guidance proposal and refinement. For each generated triplet, we first construct a candidate set of prompts. During prompt-variation generation, we also prompt an LLM to identify the aspects of the images that are intended to change. If the images were fully described by the input text prompts, this would be sufficient. However, as the mapping between prompts and images is not one-to-one, images may vary from the prompt, or show additional unspecified properties. As such, we pass the triplet and the candidate list to a VLM for refinement, removing unrelated ones and adding visually-varying factors that are not explicit in the prompts (e.g., pose or object size). The resulting aspect list is intentionally over-complete, and it is not guaranteed to be aligned with how humans describe (or attend to) differences in the triplet. We therefore treat these as proposals and prune. For each triplet, we ask 5 annotators for judgments. We provide an additional “can’t tell” option, and if marked by 3 or more users, we remove the attribute from the list. From the remaining triplets we remove the “can’t tell” votes and normalize to get probability distribution 𝐲 = ( y 1 , y 2 , y 3 ) ∈ Δ 3 \mathbf{y}=(y_{1},y_{2},y_{3})\in\Delta^{3} . We also ask for overall similarity, recorded under the “overall” condition. Our final dataset is 𝒟 = { ( 𝐗 ( n ) , 𝐜 ( n ) , 𝐲 ( n ) ) } n \mathcal{D}=\{(\mathbf{X}^{(n)},\mathbf{c}^{(n)},\mathbf{y}^{(n)})\}_{n} , where each datapoint is a tuple of image triplet 𝐗 ( n ) = { 𝐱 1 ( n ) , 𝐱 2 ( n ) , 𝐱 3 ( n ) } \mathbf{X}^{(n)}=\{\mathbf{x}_{1}^{(n)},\mathbf{x}_{2}^{(n)},\mathbf{x}_{3}^{(n)}\} , aspect condition 𝐜 ( n ) \mathbf{c}^{(n)} , and human vote distribution 𝐲 ( n ) \mathbf{y}^{(n)} . sections.heading: 3.2 Out-of-distribution 2AFC dataset
sections.text: To test generalization to different image variations and content, we curate an additional out-of-distribution evaluation set from the outputs of other computer vision algorithms. This choice is motivated by a practical use case of our framework—evaluating and comparing vision systems—and by the fact that algorithm outputs provide structured, perceptually meaningful variations. Unlike our main dataset, this setting is inherently reference-based : each query comes with a reference image (either the algorithm input or the ground-truth target) and multiple candidate outputs. We therefore adopt a 2-alternative-forced-choice (2AFC) protocol: given an aspect 𝐜 \mathbf{c} , annotators are shown the reference 𝐱 ref \mathbf{x}_{\text{ref}} and two randomly sampled outputs ( 𝐱 0 , 𝐱 1 ) (\mathbf{x}_{0},\mathbf{x}_{1}) , and select which output is more similar to the reference under 𝐜 \mathbf{c} , with multiple votes across annotators averaged as y ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] y\in[0,1] . Similar to the odd-one-out dataset, we collect votes across 5 annotators and remove those with ≥ 3 \geq 3 “can’t tell” votes. We also remove datapoints that have a tie, as they are not useful for evaluation. This produces an evaluation dataset 𝒟 ext = { ( 𝐱 ref , 𝐱 0 , 𝐱 1 , 𝐜 , y ) } \mathcal{D}_{\text{ext}}=\{(\mathbf{x}_{\text{ref}},\mathbf{x}_{0},\mathbf{x}_{1},\mathbf{c},y)\} . The external algorithms and domains used in this out-of-distribution set differ from the training data; an overview of dataset statistics is in Table 1 . Additional details are in Appendix A .

sections.heading: 4.2 Architecture
sections.text: Vision-language models (VLMs) are a natural starting point, as one can prompt a VLM to judge the similarity of two images along a given text condition. However, we find a substantial gap between current VLMs’ zero-shot judgments and human perceptual choices (Section 5 ), motivating task-specific fine-tuning. As shown in Figure 3 (right), we explore three architectures that differ in how early the two images interact in the network, ranging from no interaction (late fusion) to full joint attention (early fusion). All three are trained end-to-end with our loss (Equation 2 ). Late fusion (embeddings). We repurpose the VLM as a text-guided embedding model, following recent work on instruction-tuned VLM retrievers [ 67 , 68 ] . Given an image 𝐱 \mathbf{x} and an aspect 𝐜 \mathbf{c} , we form the prompt “ Represent the similarity of the image based on < 𝐜 \mathbf{c} > ” and feed it together with 𝐱 \mathbf{x} into the VLM, taking the final, normalized hidden state of the last token as the embedding 𝐳 = g ^ θ ​ ( 𝐱 , 𝐜 ) \mathbf{z}=\widehat{g}_{\theta}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{c}) . Pairwise similarity is then the cosine of the two embeddings: f θ ​ ( 𝐱 1 , 𝐱 2 ∣ 𝐜 ) = g ^ θ ​ ( 𝐱 1 , 𝐜 ) ⊤ ​ g ^ θ ​ ( 𝐱 2 , 𝐜 ) f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{1},\mathbf{x}_{2}\mid\mathbf{c})=\widehat{g}_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{1},\mathbf{c})^{\!\top}\,\widehat{g}_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{2},\mathbf{c}) . This is efficient at inference time, as embeddings can be precomputed and cached. As the two images never interact within the network, the model must commit to a text-guided summary independently. sections.heading: 5 Experiments
sections.text: We evaluate on the odd-one-out and out-of-distribution 2AFC test sets. Our dataset improves VLMs on other perceptual similarity benchmarks. We discuss applications of our methods, such as aspect-conditioned retrieval and compositional retrieval, and show qualitative examples. Metrics. For each aspect in a triplet, we report models’ agreement with humans [ 2 ] , measuring how often a random rater agrees with the model’s top choice. For an odd-one-out triplet with human vote distribution 𝐲 = ( y 1 , y 2 , y 3 ) \mathbf{y}=(y_{1},y_{2},y_{3}) and model prediction k ^ = arg ⁡ max k ⁡ y ^ k \hat{k}=\arg\max_{k}\hat{y}_{k} , agreement is y k ^ y_{\hat{k}} –the probability humans vote the same as model prediction. Averaging all aspect conditions over the test set gives the expected rater–model agreement. The 2AFC analogue is defined identically over two choices. To contextualize absolute agreement numbers, we compute human consensus . It is defined as y 1 2 + y 2 2 + y 3 2 y_{1}^{2}+y_{2}^{2}+y_{3}^{2} , the expected agreement within raters for each aspect condition, averaged over the test set. This human consensus reflects the best achievable agreement; we report it alongside all agreement numbers. Likewise, the 2AFC analogue is defined identically over two choices. Baselines are organized below: • Classic : LPIPS [ 2 ] , DreamSim [ 3 ] . Apply same similarity score regardless of the queried aspect. • Late fusion (embeddings) : text-image embedding models including text-conditioned encoders (SteerViT [ 70 ] )), late mixing of text and image embeddings (GeneCIS [ 8 ] ), VLM-finetuned embedding models (VLM2Vec-2.0 [ 65 ] , Qwen3-VL-Embedding [ 17 ] ), and proprietary models (Gemini-2-Embedding [ 13 ] ). • Early fusion : VLMs including open-weight models (Qwen3-VL [ 14 ] , InternVL3.5 [ 71 ] , and LLaVA-OneVision [ 63 ] ) and proprietary models (GPT-5.4 and Gemini 3.1 Pro). Each model is given both images and the text prompt and asked to return a scalar value within [ 0 , 10 ] [0,10] . • Mid-fusion (activation difference) : we find that Qwen3-VL series is the best performing open-weight backbone in both late and early fusion, and focus on this family for the mid-fusion analysis. Extended comparisons are detailed in Table 3 . We present our main results in Figure 5 . On our odd-one-out task, a substantial gap exists between the human consensus ( 67.5 % 67.5\% , with 33.3 % 33.3\% chance) and baseline model predictions across both tasks. LPIPS ( 46.2 % 46.2\% ) and DreamSim ( 50.5 % 50.5\% ) are aspect-agnostic, and merely providing an overall similarity judgement is not sufficient. Among baselines, Gemini-3.1-Pro achieves the highest model-human agreement on the odd-one-out task at 58.4 % 58.4\% . Among open-weight models, the embedding-based Qwen3-VL-Embed performs best on both tasks, and we therefore adopt it as the backbone for our approach. Fine-tuning on our data substantially narrows the gap to the human consensus, reducing it from 9.1 % 9.1\% to 2.8 % 2.8\% on the odd-one-out task. Notably, these gains translate to the held-out 2AFC distribution, reducing error from 15.8 % 15.8\% to 10.0 % 10.0\% , above baselines. The larger gap leaves more room for improvement relative to the in-domain odd-one-out test set. Figure 4 shows qualitative examples. Figure 6 : Video example. Similarity between video frames to the initial frame. While the overall similarity is dominated by the main factors (camera angle, as well as sunshine), the metric can be steered to different attributes, such as the cup handle position. Figure 7 : Aspect-conditioned Image Retrieval. Given a query on the left, our method retrieves images with respect to different visual aspects. Each row represents an aspect. Compared to the base model (Qwen-VL-8B-Embedding), our fine-tuned late-fusion model consistently retrieves images that better match the specified aspects. To encourage retrieval diversity, we adjust the ranking score by subtracting a fraction of the overall similarity from the aspect similarity. We also include retrieval results without this adjustment in Appendix B.1 . Figure 8 : Compositional retrieval. Each query is specified with different aspects, and we directly sum up similarity scores from two queries to rank the data. For example, combining (1) the painting of two sitting people conditioned on subject matter and (2) Monet’s painting conditioned on brush work yields Impressionist paintings of two sitting people. When we swap out the second query to be color-palette specific, we can retrieve portraits of two people in the same pink and blue color tone. Early, mid, and late-fusion. Among the baseline models, no single fusion strategy consistently dominates. The comparisons are not direct as they are trained with various settings. Mid-fusion performs relatively poorly for off-the-shelf baselines, as such models are not designed to produce informative mid-level features directly. In the controlled setting where we fine-tune all model types under the same base model, early fusion consistently outperforms both middle and late fusion, albeit by a modest margin. This suggests that allowing the model to interact with both images from the earliest layers is beneficial for perceptual similarity judgements. On the other hand, the late fusion model achieves similar performance but enables efficient retrieval by precomputing embeddings. We will present our results mainly with the late fusion model unless specified. We analyze the effect of dataset scale and model size in more detail in Appendix B.2 . Qualitative video example. In Fig 6 , we show a synthesized video of a camera rotating around a teacup, and calculate our metric from each frame to the initial frame. The main factors that vary is the “camera angle”, as well as “sunshine” that appears in the middle of the video. As such, the “overall” similarity mirrors these two main factors. However, the metric can be prompted to completely different factors. The “number of cups” stays nearly constant, while “number of spoons” drops when the spoon disappears behind the cup. More dramatically, prompting for the “cup handle position” causes a large perturbation, as the handle moves from the right to left side. Aspect-conditioned retrieval. Figure 7 illustrates how our method can retrieve perceptually similar images under different aspect conditions given the same query. We index the OpenImages [ 72 ] training set (1.7M images) and retrieve nearest neighbors conditioned on each aspect independently. We encourage the retrieval for each aspect to have more different-looking images by adjusting the similarity score to f θ ​ ( 𝐱 1 , 𝐱 2 ∣ 𝐜 aspect ) − 0.3 ∗ f θ ​ ( 𝐱 1 , 𝐱 2 ∣ 𝐜 overall ) f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{1},\mathbf{x}_{2}\mid\mathbf{c_{\text{aspect}}})-0.3*f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{1},\mathbf{x}_{2}\mid\mathbf{c_{\text{overall}}}) , where 𝐜 aspect \mathbf{c_{\text{aspect}}} and 𝐜 overall \mathbf{c_{\text{overall}}} represent aspect and overall condition, respectively. The results clearly demonstrate that perceptual similarity is context-dependent. The same query yields meaningfully different nearest neighbors depending on the aspect condition. We provide retrieval results without the similarity adjustments in Appendix B.1 . Compositional retrieval. Our method supports compositional queries by linearly combining similarity scores across multiple queries conditioned on different aspect conditions. We validate this on OpenImages again, and we also show results on the WikiArt dataset [ 73 ] (800K images), where aspects such as subject matter, brushwork, and color palette capture independently meaningful dimensions of visual similarity. As shown in Figure 8 , composing queries across different aspects produces retrievals that jointly satisfy all specified conditions, and swapping a single query component leads to interpretably different results. We provide more qualitative results in Appendix B.1 .

sections.heading: 6 Discussion, Broader Impacts, and Limitations
sections.text: Beyond using our metric as a human-grained, aspect-conditioned judge, it can serve as a feedback signal to improve them, as recent work has leveraged VLM feedback to train image editing [ 74 , 75 ] and generation [ 37 , 76 ] models. Our method can also aid in interpretability systems that automatically discover and characterize neural features [ 77 , 78 ] . Our metric offers human-aligned measurements to assess which fine-grained visual properties the discovered features encode. As generative and perceptual vision systems see broader deployment, interpretability becomes essential for public oversight, accountability, and informed regulation. Our VLM-based metric is substantially more expensive to compute than LPIPS or DreamSim. Also, our current embedding-based retrieval requires separate feature encoding and indexing for each aspect condition. In addition, our annotator pool is not representative of all viewers; perception varies across people, and our metric inherits that bias. Our method is also limited by training data diversity. We source prompts from FLUX-Reason-6M [ 66 ] , which has more aesthetically curated images. Our aspect proposals are VLM-generated, and we can systematically miss aspects that VLMs cannot capture. Since our triplets often share similar semantic content, our learned metric is not fully disentangled from the original content (e.g., sunny beach images will have higher weather similarity scores on other similar sunny beach images than sunny forest images). Data-related issues could be addressed with more diverse image sources and human-annotated aspects in future work. That said, as VLMs continue to improve, our pipeline naturally benefits — and we view our human perceptual data as a complementary signal toward building more human-aligned models, offering a new angle for collecting fine-grained human perceptual judgments. sections.heading: Appendix A Dataset collection and curation
sections.text: We extend Section 3 and provide the full curation pipeline behind the synthetic odd-one-out dataset used for training and in-distribution evaluation (Section A.1 ), and the vision-algorithm 2AFC set used for out-of-distribution evaluation (Section A.2 ). Throughout, we use the term aspect for the text condition 𝐜 \mathbf{c} (e.g., lighting , color tone , scene geometry ). Annotation crowdsourcing. We collect annotations on Amazon Mechanical Turk and Prolific. Reward per task is set to target an effective hourly rate of $10/hour. Sentinel checks are applied to every session. A sentinel triplet is constructed by duplicating one image from a real triplet, making the correct odd-one-out visually unambiguous. Sessions that fail the sentinels are returned, and the corresponding responses are excluded. Per-aspect “can’t tell” filter. To handle the case where the visual aspect condition is ambiguous, our annotation interface includes a “can’t tell” option in addition to the image choices. We collect 5 annotations per triplet, discard the “can’t tell” vote, and only train and test on the image votes. To ensure sufficient votes for all visual aspects in the test set, we discard any aspect if 3 or more annotators mark “can’t tell” in the test set. The filter is applied independently per aspect. A triplet may keep some aspects and lose others, and we drop the triplet only when no aspect remains.

sections.heading: A.1 Odd-one-out dataset
sections.text: Image generation. We use the FLUX-Reason-6M [ 66 ] caption pool as base prompts. For each base prompt, an instruction-tuned LLM (Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 [ 79 ] ) authors three controlled prompt variations along a small set of pre-specified axes (e.g., color, lighting, composition), so that within a triplet the three prompts deliberately differ on at least one axis. The three prompts are then rendered by FLUX.1-dev [ 80 ] with a shared random seed, 50 sampling steps, and guidance scale of 4.0 4.0 . Below are the instructions to generate the prompt variation: System Prompt You are an expert at generating perceptual variations for odd-one-out perceptual studies. TASK: Given a base text prompt, generate THREE CLEARLY DISTINGUISHABLE text-to-image prompts (0, 1, 2) that form an interesting odd-one-out triplet. GOAL: These images will be shown to humans who must identify which image is "most different" from the others. For each visual FACTOR you vary, TWO images should be SIMILAR and ONE should be the "ODD" one (clearly different). CRITICAL DESIGN PRINCIPLES: 1. Vary 5-7 visual factors across the triplet 2. For EACH factor: two images share a similar value, one image is distinctly different 3. DISTRIBUTE the "odd" role across images - don’t make one image odd for all factors! - Example: Image 0 might be odd for "lighting" and "pose" - Image 1 might be odd for "background" and "texture" - Image 2 might be odd for "camera angle" and "color" 4. This creates an INTERESTING perceptual puzzle where each image is "odd" in some ways but "similar" in others VISUAL FACTORS TO VARY (use contextual names, not category names): - Color & Illumination → "lighting warmth", "shadow direction", "brightness level" - Material & Texture → "sofa fabric", "surface glossiness", "wood grain" - Geometry & Shape & Pose → "cat pose", "flower arrangement", "building height" - Background & Environment → "sky condition", "room clutter", "weather" - Composition & Spatial Arrangement → "object spacing", "framing tightness" - Camera → "camera distance", "viewing angle", "depth of field" - Photographic Style → "color saturation", "film grain", "contrast level" REQUIREMENTS: 1. All three must describe the same subject(s) or scene 2. Use VIVID, SPECIFIC descriptors - avoid "slightly" or "somewhat" 3. Each prompt should produce an image DISTINGUISHABLE AT A GLANCE 4. Factor names must be contextual: "cat pose" not "Geometry & Shape" 5. Keep factor names short and understandable by non-experts EXAMPLE for "A golden retriever in a park": { "metadata": { "num_variations": 3, "factors": [ {"name": "dog pose", "odd_image": 0, "similar_value": "sitting upright", "odd_value": "lying down"}, {"name": "lighting", "odd_image": 1, "similar_value": "bright sunny", "odd_value": "overcast diffuse"}, {"name": "background trees", "odd_image": 2, "similar_value": "lush green", "odd_value": "autumn orange"}, {"name": "grass length", "odd_image": 0, "similar_value": "short manicured", "odd_value": "tall wild"}, {"name": "camera angle", "odd_image": 1, "similar_value": "eye level", "odd_value": "low angle looking up"}, {"name": "depth of field", "odd_image": 2, "similar_value": "sharp throughout", "odd_value": "blurred background"} ] }, "triplets": [ {"id": 0, "prompt_or_edit_or_video_instruction": "A golden retriever lying down in tall wild grass in a sunny park with lush green trees, eye level shot, sharp focus throughout, bright natural lighting"}, {"id": 1, "prompt_or_edit_or_video_instruction": "A golden retriever sitting upright in short manicured grass in a park under overcast diffuse light, low angle looking up, lush green trees, sharp focus throughout"}, {"id": 2, "prompt_or_edit_or_video_instruction": "A golden retriever sitting upright in short manicured grass in a sunny park with autumn orange trees, eye level shot, blurred background, bright natural lighting"} ] } OUTPUT FORMAT: Return ONLY valid JSON with the structure shown above. Remember: Make each image "odd" for roughly 2-3 factors, creating an interesting perceptual puzzle! Aspect proposal and refinement. Each triplet inherits the proposed aspects from its prompt-variation step. Because the prompt-to-image mapping is not faithful, we additionally pass the rendered triplet and its candidate aspect list to GPT-5.2 [ 12 ] and ask it to drop aspects that are not visibly varying across the three images and to add visually salient aspects that the prompts did not specify. The refinement instruction is: System Prompt You are analyzing three horizontally concatenated images (left, middle, right). INITIAL AXES OF VARIATION: <list of aspects inserted here> TASK: Refine the initial axes based on the images. Keep most axes, remove only irrelevant ones, and add any new axes for visual differences that are actually present. RULES (must be strictly followed): 1. Each axis must be a single, concise noun phrase. 2. Do NOT use the words "and", "or", "not", parentheses, asterisks, commas, or any other symbols in an axis. 3. Always name axes contextually for the subject (e.g., "cat pose", "sky brightness", "table material"). 4. Always include axes for pose, orientation, geometry, size, or viewpoint if subjects vary. 5. Include axes for color, lighting, material, texture, background, composition, camera, or photographic style if relevant. 6. Output only axes that actually vary between the images. 7. Do not hallucinate axes that are not visually evident. 8. Provide 5-10 axes sorted by importance, most important first. OUTPUT FORMAT: Numbered list 1. [Most important axis] 2. [Second axis] 3. ... The output is an over-complete refined aspect list, which is then pruned by the can’t-tell filter from human annotation. Annotation interface. Annotators see three triangle-arranged images and a list of refined aspects rendered as draggable chips. For each aspect, they drag the chip onto the image they consider the odd-one-out, or onto a “can’t tell” bin (Figure 9 ). Each triplet is annotated by 5 workers; after the can’t-tell filter, the remaining votes form a categorical distribution 𝐲 ∈ Δ 3 \mathbf{y}\in\Delta^{3} over the three image positions. We additionally include one “overall” aspect per triplet by asking an unconditional question “which image looks most different overall?”. We treat “overall” as a regular aspect condition during training and evaluation. Figure 9 : Odd-one-out annotation interface. Annotators are shown three images. (Left) Annotators click the most different-looking image overall. (Right) Annotators are given a list of aspects as draggable chips, and assign each aspect either to the image they perceive as the odd-one-out or to “can’t tell”.

sections.text: Table 2 : Algorithms and aspects used in the 2AFC set. We report the algorithms used for our 2AFC set and the number of triplet occurrences for each algorithm, along with the aspect list used. Source Algorithm (# triplets it appears in) Aspect list Image editing BAGEL (67), FLUX2-dev (83), LongCat-Image-Edit (72), OmniGen2 (92), Qwen-Image-Edit (64), Qwen-Image-Edit-2511 (69), Step1X-Edit v1.2 (65) 6–10 aspects predicted by GPT-5.2 per sample and human-pruned Image compositing IC-Light (197), DreamLight (195), Diff-Harmonization (196) (fg-ref) facial features, hair texture, clothing detail; (bg-ref) lighting direction, lighting warmth, color tone, illumination Novel view synthesis Splatfacto (120), Nerfacto (120), Instant-NGP (120) scene geometry, scene sharpness, texture detail, color tone, lighting brightness Single-image 3D TRELLIS.2-4B (197), InstantMesh (199), Hunyuan3D-2.1 (199), Step1X-3D (199) 3D shape, surface texture, material, color tone, camera pose, object size Figure 10 : 2AFC annotation interface. Annotators see a reference image (center) and two candidates on two sides and select, for each aspect, which candidate is more similar to the reference, or “can’t tell”. The 2AFC set is curated from outputs of real vision algorithms across four sources: image editing, image compositing, novel view synthesis (NVS), and single-image 3D. Each source contributes a reference image 𝐱 ref \mathbf{x}_{\text{ref}} and outputs from multiple algorithms; a triplet pairs 𝐱 ref \mathbf{x}_{\text{ref}} with two outputs from different algorithms, and the annotator picks the output more similar to 𝐱 ref \mathbf{x}_{\text{ref}} for each aspect. Algorithms and aspect lists per source are summarized in Table 2 . Image editing. Sources are drawn from GEditBench v2 [ 81 ] , which includes 16 methods. We keep the 7 methods: BAGEL [ 82 ] , FLUX2-dev [ 83 ] , LongCat-Image-Edit [ 84 ] , OmniGen2 [ 85 ] , Qwen-Image-Edit [ 86 ] , Qwen-Image-Edit-2511 [ 86 ] , Step1X-Edit v1.2 [ 87 ] ). The rest are dropped either because they crop or resize the input on at least some samples or because they are near-duplicate intermediate releases of one of the kept models. We further discard four edit categories from GEditBench v2 (chart editing, in-image text translation, text editing, and line-to-image) since they contains visual content out of our interest (e.g., text renders, charts, line sketches). For each sample, GPT-5.2 names the target aspect that the edit instruction explicitly changes (e.g., background setting for the instruction “replace the background with a modern office”) and 6–10 preserved aspects that should remain identical to the reference; both lists are then human-pruned. Both target and preserved aspects are kept in the annotation list. Each triplet pairs the source photograph with two edits from different, random-selected methods of the same instruction. We drop triplets whose human majority votes are the same image for every aspect, since these are usually dominated by one method barely modifying the input. Image compositing. We use 10 foreground images of portraits crossed with 30 background reference photographs and run three methods on each pair: IC-Light (text-foreground-background-conditioned model) [ 88 ] , DreamLight [ 89 ] , and zero-shot Diff-Harmonization [ 90 ] . Each foreground-background pair yields two reference modes: foreground-reference (the foreground is 𝐱 ref \mathbf{x}_{\text{ref}} and the aspects describe subject preservation) and background-reference (the background photograph is 𝐱 ref \mathbf{x}_{\text{ref}} , and the aspects describe background preservation). We take random subsets from this collection to ensure the dataset size matches the other tasks. Novel view synthesis. We use 6 scenes from Mip-NeRF 360 [ 91 ] and 3 nerfstudio methods [ 92 ] : Splatfacto (3D Gaussian Splatting [ 93 ] ), Nerfacto [ 94 ] , and Instant-NGP [ 95 ] . All methods receive the same training views and render the same held-out poses; the reference image is the held-out ground-truth photograph at the test pose. Single-image 3D. We use inputs from 3D Arena and 4 methods: TRELLIS.2 [ 96 ] , InstantMesh [ 97 ] , Hunyuan3D-2.1 [ 98 ] , and Step1X-3D [ 99 ] . Each method’s mesh is re-rendered in Blender at 4 spaced-out azimuth angles per object; the reference image is the source photograph. Since there is no consistent canonical view for each method, camera poses from each method are randomly different from the reference. Hence, we also annotate and evaluate camera pose similarity in this setting. Annotation interface. Each triplet is presented as [ 𝐱 cand A ​ ∣ 𝐱 ref ∣ ​ 𝐱 cand B ] [\mathbf{x}_{\text{cand A}}\mid\mathbf{x}_{\text{ref}}\mid\mathbf{x}_{\text{cand B}}] , with the reference in the center. Per triplet, annotators are shown the aspect list and select, for each aspect, which candidate is more similar to the reference, or “can’t tell” (Figure 10 ). Each (triplet, aspect) is annotated by 5 workers, and we apply the “can’t-tell” filter as before. Following Section 3.2 , we additionally drop aspects whose post-filter vote is exactly tied. Unlike the odd-one-out evaluation, the 2AFC evaluation does not include an “overall” aspect: every comparison is explicitly conditioned on a visual aspect.

sections.heading: B.1 Additional analysis and benchmarks
sections.text: Table 3 includes analysis from more models, measured by their agreement with humans. Triplet oracle. Section 5 reports evaluation on pairwise metrics. Our goal is to create an algorithm that can judge pairwise distance, using the odd-one-out triplet task as a pretext training signal. Here, though the odd-one-out task is not the primary task, as an advantaged “oracle”, we provide all 3 images to the VLM, and see how closely our pairwise algorithm (which only sees 2 images at a time) compares. To do so, we ask the model: “Which image is the most different among the three in terms of <aspect> ?”, same as what the human annotators answered. This makes even untrained VLMs strong baselines under the triplet prompt. While Gemini-3.1-Pro reaches 62.0 % 62.0\% on odd-one-out and GPT-5.4 reaches 77.9 % 77.9\% total on 2AFC, our early fusion method still outperforms even without the structural advantage. In addition, we verify that finetuning a generative VLM to solve the odd-one-out task directly with the triplet yields the strongest result (see Ours-Triplet). However, such a model produces only a triplet decision and not a pairwise score, and therefore does not transfer to 2AFC evaluation and retrieval. The pairwise design is what makes the metric usable across all of these settings. Effect of model size. As expected, for most model families, agreement with humans increases with backbone size on both the in-distribution odd-one-out test and the 2AFC total. For example, in early fusion baselines, InternVL3.5 climbs 45.4 % → 54.2 % 45.4\%\to 54.2\% from 1B to 14B, and Qwen3-VL climbs 51.0 % → 54.5 % 51.0\%\to 54.5\% from 2B to 8B. In our ablation studies (Section B.2 ), we also find that our method’s performance improves with model size (Table 6 ). Our model maintains the smallest gap to human-human agreement at every τ \tau , demonstrating that its advantage is not threshold-sensitive. sections.text: In this section, we include training and hyperparameter details (Section C.1 ), architecture details for our early fusion model (Section C.2 ), and baseline details (Section C.3 ).

sections.heading: C.1 Training and hyperparameter selection
sections.text: Backbones. The late-fusion, mid-fusion, and early-fusion variants of our model all use Qwen3-VL-Embedding-8B [ 17 ] as the backbone. The triplet generative variant uses Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct [ 14 ] . Adaptation. We apply LoRA [ 69 ] to the language tower with lora_alpha = 2 ⋅ lora_r \text{lora\_alpha}=2\cdot\text{lora\_r} and dropout 0.05 0.05 . The vision tower is frozen for all reported models, as we find that tuning the vision tower doesn’t improve performance. Optimizer and schedule. We optimize using AdamW (weight decay 0.01 0.01 , gradient clipping 1.0 1.0 ). The learning-rate schedule is a linear warmup over 3 % 3\% of total steps followed by cosine decay to zero [ 100 ] . The triplet variant uses two parameter groups: backbone LoRA at the listed learning rate and the classification head at 5 × 5\times that rate. Data and per-step batching. All four models are trained on the unfiltered training split (22,157 triplets) for one epoch. Each aspect in a triplet is treated as one training example, so a triplet annotated for k k aspects contributes k k optimization examples per epoch. Per-device batch size is 1 1 ; the effective batch size is per-device batch size times gradient accumulation times eight GPUs, since our training is done on 8-GPU nodes. Permutation augmentation for triplet models. To alleviate position bias of vision language models [ 101 , 102 , 103 ] , when training triplet models, the three images of every triplet are randomly permuted per batch item. At inference, we average over all six permutations and map probabilities back to the original positions. Model prompts. The aspect string 𝐜 \mathbf{c} is inserted into the following prompts. For late fusion and mid fusion (one image per forward pass): “Represent the similarity of the image based on ⟨ 𝐜 ⟩ \langle\,\mathbf{c}\,\rangle .” For early fusion (two images per forward pass): “Measure the similarity between the two images based on ⟨ 𝐜 ⟩ \langle\,\mathbf{c}\,\rangle .” The “overall” aspect drops the “based on ⟨ 𝐜 ⟩ \langle\,\mathbf{c}\,\rangle ” suffix. Hyperparameter sweep. We run an independent Bayesian search per family with validation human agreement as the target. sections.heading: C.2 Early-fusion architecture
sections.text: We describe the attention mask and positional encoding scheme that make the early-fusion architecture (Section 4.2 ) symmetric and identity-preserving by construction. Input layout. The input sequence consists of four contiguous segments, with the aspect prompt first so that image patches can attend to it in the standard VLM fashion: 𝐭 1 , … , 𝐭 M ⏟ aspect tokens ​ 𝐜 | 𝐩 1 ( 1 ) , … , 𝐩 N ( 1 ) ⏟ image ​ 𝐱 1 ​ patches ​ ‖ 𝐩 1 ( 2 ) , … , 𝐩 N ( 2 ) ⏟ image ​ 𝐱 2 ​ patches ‖ ​ 𝐫 1 , 𝐫 2 ⏟ registers , \underbrace{\mathbf{t}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{t}_{M}}_{\text{aspect tokens }\mathbf{c}}\;\|\;\underbrace{\mathbf{p}^{(1)}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{p}^{(1)}_{N}}_{\text{image }\mathbf{x}_{1}\text{ patches}}\;\|\;\underbrace{\mathbf{p}^{(2)}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{p}^{(2)}_{N}}_{\text{image }\mathbf{x}_{2}\text{ patches}}\;\|\;\underbrace{\mathbf{r}_{1},\mathbf{r}_{2}}_{\text{registers}}, where 𝐭 m \mathbf{t}_{m} are the aspect text token embeddings, 𝐩 n ( k ) \mathbf{p}^{(k)}_{n} denotes the n n -th patch embedding of image 𝐱 k \mathbf{x}_{k} (we assume both images have the same number of patches N N ), and 𝐫 1 , 𝐫 2 \mathbf{r}_{1},\mathbf{r}_{2} are shared-parameter learnable register vectors shared across all examples. Positional encoding. We use M-RoPE [ 60 ] , which assigns each token a three-dimensional position ( t , h , w ) (t,h,w) . For vision tokens we override the backbone default so that both images share the same temporal index and matching spatial indices at corresponding grid locations: pos ⁡ ( 𝐩 h , w ( 1 ) ) = pos ⁡ ( 𝐩 h , w ( 2 ) ) = ( 0 , h , w ) , \mathrm{pos}\bigl(\mathbf{p}^{(1)}_{h,w}\bigr)=\mathrm{pos}\bigl(\mathbf{p}^{(2)}_{h,w}\bigr)=(0,\,h,\,w), where ( h , w ) (h,w) follow each image’s patch grid after preprocessing. Hence, the two images are distinguished only by token content and by the attention mask, not by the image ordering. The aspect text is assigned sequential temporal positions t = 1 , 2 , … t=1,2,\ldots in sequence order, with ( h , w ) = ( 0 , 0 ) (h,w)=(0,0) , while reserving t = 0 t=0 for all vision patches—this differs from default two-image preprocessing in which the second image often receives a larger temporal index. Registers. The two registers use the same learnable embedding vector and the same M-RoPE coordinates ( t reg , 0 , 0 ) (t_{\mathrm{reg}},0,0) with t reg t_{\mathrm{reg}} set immediately after the maximum temporal index among all preceding tokens. They are therefore not distinguished by positional encoding; only their attention regions differ, as illustrated below. Attention mask. The attention mask is defined by the following rules: 1. Aspect tokens are causal among themselves and hence attend to no image patches or registers, preserving the pretrained text-only behavior of the VLM. 2. Image patches attend to all aspect tokens and to all image patches of both images, encouraging comparisons between two sets of image features. They do not attend to the registers. 3. Registers are restricted: 𝐫 k \mathbf{r}_{k} attends to the aspect tokens and to the patches of image 𝐱 k \mathbf{x}_{k} only. This encourages 𝐫 k \mathbf{r}_{k} to output an image-specific representation. The image-image block of the mask is symmetric, and the register block is symmetric in the analogous sense: 𝐫 1 \mathbf{r}_{1} ’s access pattern to 𝐱 1 \mathbf{x}_{1} mirrors 𝐫 2 \mathbf{r}_{2} ’s access pattern to 𝐱 2 \mathbf{x}_{2} . Symmetry property. The two registers 𝐫 1 , 𝐫 2 \mathbf{r}_{1},\mathbf{r}_{2} share the same learned embedding and the same positional encoding, and the attention mask treats the two image slots symmetrically. So if we swap 𝐱 1 \mathbf{x}_{1} and 𝐱 2 \mathbf{x}_{2} , at every attention layer 𝐫 1 \mathbf{r}_{1} now pools from 𝐱 2 \mathbf{x}_{2} exactly as 𝐫 2 \mathbf{r}_{2} did before (and vice versa); the two register hidden states are simply exchanged. Since cosine similarity is symmetric in its arguments, f θ ​ ( 𝐱 1 , 𝐱 2 , 𝐜 ) = f θ ​ ( 𝐱 2 , 𝐱 1 , 𝐜 ) . f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{1},\mathbf{x}_{2},\mathbf{c})=f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{2},\mathbf{x}_{1},\mathbf{c}). Identity property. When 𝐱 1 = 𝐱 2 = 𝐱 \mathbf{x}_{1}=\mathbf{x}_{2}=\mathbf{x} , the two image segments of the input sequence are token-for-token identical and the attention mask is symmetric, so the two segments produce identical hidden states at every transformer layer. Since 𝐫 1 \mathbf{r}_{1} and 𝐫 2 \mathbf{r}_{2} are tied and attend to identical contexts via structurally identical masks, 𝐡 1 = 𝐡 2 \mathbf{h}_{1}=\mathbf{h}_{2} . Hence f θ ​ ( 𝐱 , 𝐱 , 𝐜 ) = 𝐡 1 ⊤ ​ 𝐡 1 ∥ 𝐡 1 ∥ 2 = 1 . f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x},\mathbf{c})=\frac{\mathbf{h}_{1}^{\!\top}\mathbf{h}_{1}}{\lVert\mathbf{h}_{1}\rVert^{2}}=1.

sections.heading: C.3 Baselines
sections.text: We provide more details of the baselines reported in Section 5 . We organize baselines by how the two images interact, plus a separate triplet family that consumes three concatenated images at once. All baselines use greedy decoding (temperature 0 0 ). To avoid position bias of VLMs [ 101 , 102 , 103 ] , for triplet and pairwise-score baselines we apply permutation averaging—6 orderings for odd-one-out, 2 for 2AFC—and map results back to the original positions. Embedding baselines do not need permutation averaging because cosine similarity is symmetric. Triplet baselines. The three input images are concatenated horizontally and the model is asked which side is the odd one out. We use the prompt: “I provide three horizontally concatenated images (left, middle, right). Which image is the most different among the three in terms of ⟨ 𝐜 ⟩ \langle\,\mathbf{c}\,\rangle ? You need to choose: left, middle, right. Answer:” For 2AFC the three positions become reference (center) and two candidates (left, right): “I provide three horizontally concatenated images. The center image is the reference. Which candidate (left or right) is more similar to the reference in terms of ⟨ 𝐜 ⟩ \langle\,\mathbf{c}\,\rangle ? Answer with one word: left or right. Answer:” When the aspect condition is “overall”, we remove “in terms of ⟨ 𝐜 ⟩ \langle\,\mathbf{c}\,\rangle ” in these prompts. For open-weight models, we read logits at the answer position for the three (resp. two) target tokens and softmax. Models include InternVL3.5 [ 71 ] , Qwen3-VL [ 14 ] , and LLaVA-OneVision [ 63 ] . API models (GPT-5.4 [ 12 ] , Gemini 3.1 Pro [ 13 ] ) use text parsing. Pairwise 0–10 score baselines. The same VLMs are also evaluated in a pairwise mode, where each pair of images is rated for similarity on an integer scale of 0 0 (completely different) to 10 10 (identical). The prompt is: “I show you two images placed side by side (left and right). Rate how similar these two images are in terms of ⟨ 𝐜 ⟩ \langle\,\mathbf{c}\,\rangle on a scale of 0 to 10, where 0 means completely different and 10 means identical. Answer with a single number from 0 to 10. Answer:” When the aspect is “overall”, we swap out “in terms of ⟨ 𝐜 ⟩ \langle\,\mathbf{c}\,\rangle ” to “overall” in the prompt. We convert the response to a soft score either as 𝔼 ⁡ [ d ] = ∑ d = 0 10 d ⋅ P ⁡ ( d ) \mathbb{E}[d]=\sum_{d=0}^{10}d\cdot P(d) over digit-token logprobs. For API calls where we can only obtain the generated text, each text response is converted to a one-hot delta distribution over choices. The three pairwise scores per triplet are converted to a 3-way odd-one-out distribution by softmaxing the complementary-pair score (so the highest similarity between two images implies the third is the odd one out); for 2AFC we softmax the two reference–candidate scores. Late-fusion (embedding) baselines. Each image is embedded independently, optionally conditioned on a short aspect prompt; pairwise similarity is the cosine of the two embeddings. The 3-way odd-one-out and 2AFC distributions are formed by the same softmax aggregation as the pairwise-score baselines. Qwen3-VL-Embedding [ 17 ] (2B and 8B). The natively multimodal encoder version of Qwen3-VL with last-token pooling and L2-normalized output. We use the prompt “ Represent the visual similarity of this image in terms of ⟨ 𝐜 ⟩ \langle\,\mathbf{c}\,\rangle . ”. VLM2Vec v2.0 [ 16 , 65 ] . A LoRA adapter on top of Qwen2-VL-2B-Instruct [ 60 ] , used as released. We use the same prompt as Qwen3-VL-Embedding and pool the last non-pad hidden state. SteerViT [ 70 ] . A DINOv2-based ViT [ 23 ] augmented with steerable cross-attention that consumes a short aspect string. SteerViT’s text encoder is RoBERTa [ 104 ] rather than an instruction-tuned LLM, so the verbose embedding prompt above is shortened to the aspect token only (e.g., “ lighting ”). For the “overall” aspect we pass no text, which falls back to the unconditional DINOv2 backbone. GeneCIS [ 8 ] . A CLIP ViT-B/16 [ 22 ] fine-tuned on conditional image-similarity triplets mined from existing vision-language datasets. As with SteerViT, CLIP’s text encoder is short-text-friendly rather than instruction-tuned, so we feed the aspect token directly (e.g., “ lighting ”). Gemini Embedding 2 [ 13 ] . The natively multimodal embedding model, used via the official API. We interleave the aspect text and the image bytes inside a single content object so the embedding is aspect-conditioned. Mid-fusion baseline. For completeness we report a frozen Qwen3-VL-Embedding (2B and 8B) used in the LPIPS-style mid-fusion configuration: pairwise similarity is the negative aspect-conditioned ℓ 2 \ell_{2} distance over selected language-tower layers (Equation 3 ). This is the same architectural class as our trained mid-fusion variant but without the trained channel-weight head, and isolates the contribution of training.

sections.heading: D.1 Compute cost
sections.text: All training and inference reported in this paper were run on eight NVIDIA A100 80GB nodes. We describe the runtime cost below. Dataset construction. Curating the odd-one-out dataset took around 24 GPU days for FLUX image generation and around 8 GPU days for the Qwen3 text prompt variations. Curating the 2AFC dataset took around 20 GPU hours for image compositing, 5 GPU hours for NVS, and 30 GPU hours for image-to-3D. We directly downloaded image editing results from GEditBench v2 [ 87 ] . Final model training. Per-run wall-clock on eight A100s: late fusion 4.5 hours, mid fusion 9 hours, early fusion 8 hours, triplet head 7 hours.

Efros Richard Zhang Affiliation: Adobe Research Affiliation: UC Berkeley Abstract Human visual similarity judgments are context-dependent. For example, two images may be similar in shape but distinct in color. Existing perceptual similarity metrics, however, collapse these nuances into a single scalar value, offering no mechanism to condition on specific aspects. To bridge this gap, we introduce a large-scale dataset of human similarity judgments over image triplets, where each triplet is annotated across multiple, free-form semantic aspects of similarity. Benchmarking a broad range of frontier vision-language models (VLMs) reveals a considerable performance gap compared to human annotators’ concensus. Leveraging our data, we fine-tune a VLM to produce our Text-Prompted Image Perceptual Similarity (TPIPS) metric, capturing multiple senses of visual similarity depending on the specified text prompt. We demonstrate that TPIPS aligns more closely with human perception and generalizes reliably beyond the training distribution. Finally, we show that TPIPS unlocks new capabilities in text-guided retrieval, compositional search, and the fine-grained evaluation of generative models. Our code, data, and trained models are at https://peterwang512.github.io/TPIPS . 1 Introduction Figure 1 : The Many Senses of Similarity. Given a reference image (top left), the four candidate images (top right) are similar to the reference in different ways, such as subject color, pose, ground surface, or texture. But existing visual similarity measures (L2, SSIM [ 1 ] , LPIPS [ 2 ] , Dreamsim [ 3 ] ) collapse similarity into a single scalar, and thus producing ambiguous and inconsistent results. Our Text-Prompted Image Perceptual Similarity (TPIPS) can be conditioned on a particular sense of similarity (aspect), prompt-able by free-form text. With conditioning, this visual similarity problem is no longer ambiguous, and our method selects the most similar image aligned with human perceptual judgements. A long line of psychology research has established that human similarity judgments are context-dependent [ 4 , 5 ] . The same holds for images: there are many senses of visual similarity, depending on which aspect (color, texture, illumination, semantics, style, etc) is being compared. Consider Figure 1 : given the reference cow statue image (left), it is not immediately obvious which of the four candidate images on the right is the most similar overall to the reference. However, the answer becomes clear if the similarity judgement is conditioned on a specific visual aspect , such as the cow’s color, pose, or the image background. The image processing and computer vision communities have spent decades making progress on capturing human perceptual similarity, from hand-engineered distances like SSIM and others [ 1 , 6 , 7 ] to learned metrics trained on annotated human similarity judgments, such as LPIPS [ 2 ] or DreamSim [ 3 ] . These methods, however, model similarity as a single, scalar quantity, without conditioning on the aspect of the comparison. While previous methods add a notion of conditioning by leveraging vision-language models [ 8 , 9 , 10 ] , to our knowledge, no dataset collected with human perceptual similarity judgments exists to serve as validation. To fill this gap, we collect a large-scale dataset of one million human similarity judgments over 25K image triplets. Following triplet-based protocols standard in perceptual similarity studies [ 2 , 3 , 11 ] , annotators provide relative perceptual judgements by comparing three images and indicating which are most or least similar. Different from prior work, we extend this protocol to perceptual judgements conditioned on various visual aspects. We collect 260K triplet-aspect condition combinations, where each triplet is annotated conditioned on multiple free-form visual aspects, each aspect yielding a separate set of similarity judgments. The triplets are generated using text-to-image models and designed to be challenging. If the differences between candidates are too subtle, humans cannot reliably judge similarity; if they are too coarse, the task collapses to judging overall similarity, which current models already handle. We target the middle ground, with images that differ along multiple aspects simultaneously — through fine-grained variations in properties such as color, lighting, and texture. We use this syntheic dataset to construct a benchmark and evaluate a broad set of baselines, including recent open-source and proprietary VLMs [ 12 , 13 , 14 , 15 ] and state-of-the-art multimodal embedding models [ 16 , 17 ] , revealing room for improvement. We find that even the strongest current VLM systems often do not agree with human similarity judgments on specified aspects. We carefully propose and analyze different architecture choices for tuning a VLM into an aspect-conditioned perceptual metric on our collected perceptual data. Our model, Text-Prompted Image Perceptual Similarity (TPIPS), narrows the performance gap considerably. To assess whether our metric remains reliable beyond the synthetic training distribution, we collect a second set of human similarity judgments over outputs generated by external algorithms, designed for four different vision and graphics tasks, spanning both generative and non-generative pipelines. Our model outperforms baselines in this setting too, suggesting that it can serve as a general-purpose perceptual metric for aspect-conditioned evaluation. We show several downstream applications: evaluation of generative vision models, where output and reference similarity is measured along specified visual axes, nearest-neighbor retrieval, where the same query image returns different neighbors under different aspects, and compositional retrieval, where multiple query images, each conditioned on a different visual aspect, can be combined to find images that match the criteria. Our code, data, and trained models are at https://peterwang512.github.io/TPIPS . 2 Related Works Perceptual similarity and preferences. Comparing two images is a fundamental problem in vision, with early approaches relying on hand-engineered, patch-based metrics [ 1 , 6 , 7 ] . With advances in deep image recognition [ 18 , 19 , 20 , 21 , 22 , 23 ] , learned deep features have been found to provide a more useful similarity signal than hand-engineered descriptors [ 2 , 24 , 25 , 26 , 27 ] . LPIPS [ 2 ] , PieAPP [ 28 ] , and DISTS [ 29 ] directly optimize deep features to align better with human judgments on low-level distortions. DreamSim [ 3 ] learns human perceptual judgments on synthesized images with high-level variations. Muttenthaler et al. [ 30 ] study perceptual judgments across object categories with THINGS [ 11 ] . Other works improve metric robustness to spatial shifts [ 31 ] , adversarial perturbations [ 32 ] , and arbitrary transformations [ 33 ] . Alternative metrics isolate specific attributes like style [ 34 , 35 ] or relationships between visual elements [ 36 ] . While these methods predict a single similarity score, similarity is inherently multi-faceted [ 4 ] . We address this by introducing a benchmark and model for human similarity judgements conditioned on various visual aspects. A separate but adjacent line of work uses pairwise human comparisons over generated or edited images to learn a scalar quality score over a single image [ 37 , 38 , 39 , 40 ] . In contrast, we learn from triplet judgments to model pairwise similarity conditioned on visual aspects. Conditional representation. Various research has studied learning representations of an input conditioned on different aspects. A line of work explores learning conditional representation given an explicit aspect, but assumes a fixed, finite vocabulary of conditions [ 41 , 42 , 43 , 44 , 45 ] . More recent work generalizes the condition input to free-form text, including training-free methods via vision-language models [ 46 , 47 , 48 ] and training-based methods that curate conditional supervision. GeneCIS [ 8 ] and FocalLens [ 9 ] mine attribute-difference triplets from existing vision-language datasets, while Omni-Attribute [ 10 ] bootstraps supervision from VLM-generated labels and TF-QARE [ 48 ] prompts for an image’s object, background, or style and averages the embedding of the resulting description. A parallel line of work studies context-conditional categorization [ 49 , 50 ] , and composed image retrieval [ 51 , 52 , 53 , 54 ] takes image-text inputs but uses the text to specify how the retrieved images should be different from the query image. Unlike prior conditional similarity work, we collect human similarity judgments directly under each aspect condition. This captures fine-grained relative differences not reliably present in image captions and VLM outputs, better aligning our method with human judgments than prior training-free, training-based methods and state-of-the-art VLMs. Vision-language models. Early vision-language models targeted a small number of tasks: dual-encoder contrastive models [ 22 , 55 , 56 ] such as CLIP [ 22 ] align image and text representations for retrieval and classification, while encoder-decoder models such as BLIP [ 57 , 58 ] added captioning and visual question answering. Modern instruction-tuned multimodal models including Qwen-VL series [ 59 , 60 , 14 , 61 ] and others [ 62 , 63 , 15 , 64 ] , and frontier proprietary systems such as Gemini [ 13 ] and GPT [ 12 ] —are trained on a much broader task mixtures [ 63 , 60 , 15 ] that, in some cases, also includes similarity benchmarks such as NIGHTS [ 3 ] and GeneCIS [ 8 ] . A parallel line of universal multimodal embedders, such as VLM2Vec [ 16 , 65 ] and Qwen3-VL-Embedding [ 17 ] , repurposes these backbones for instruction-conditioned retrieval. While VLMs can solve various vision tasks, we find that the performance gap remains for VLMs to yield human-aligned pairwise similarity judgments conditioned on specified aspects. Our benchmark and models aid in closing this gap. 3 Dataset collection Our goal is to collect a dataset of similarity judgments 𝒟 \mathcal{D} , such that they can be used to train and evaluate a text-conditioned similarity algorithm. Human perceptual similarity is inherently relative: given a small set of candidates (e.g., 3 images), people can reliably identify the most different item, or the closer pair, with respect to visual aspects such as lighting, object pose, or background [ 4 ] . To do so, as shown in Figure 2 , we collect two datasets: (1) a large, synthetic dataset on odd-one-out judgments, which we use for training, and (2) a smaller set on other vision and graphics algorithms to validate the generalization of our algorithm on real-world applications. 3.1 Odd-one-out dataset Given a pair of images, humans cannot reliably provide a similarity score directly, which led previous works to collect relative comparisons from image triplets by asking which of two image variations is closer to a given reference [ 2 , 3 ] , or which image is the most different [ 11 ] . In this setting, we adopt the odd-one-out task [ 11 ] , and extend it to perceptual judgements conditioned on various visual aspects. To construct our dataset, we curate a diverse yet controlled set of image variations. A core challenge lies in identifying an optimal difficulty regime: triplets must be neither trivial, where differences are too vast, nor uninformative, where differences are negligible. Furthermore, images within a single triplet must exhibit variation across multiple independent text-conditioned aspects to necessitate multi-faceted reasoning. Randomly sampling from large-scale image datasets or subsampling a video dataset typically yields degenerate triplets, where one image is an outlier across all aspects or the visual distance between the images is too great to allow for meaningful comparison. Inspired by Fu et al. [ 3 ] , we leverage text-to-image (T2I), language (LLM), and vision-language (VLM) models to propose candidate triplets and text conditionings at scale. We generate candidate triplets by sampling prompts from FLUX-Reason-6M [ 66 ] . A straightforward approach is to sample images from the same prompt, but this often fails to produce sufficiently diverse variations. As such, we use a language model to generate variations of a given prompt, before rendering the triplet. This produces a controlled yet diverse candidate set, while allowing humans to judge which of the text-induced variations are actually reflected in the images. Text guidance proposal and refinement. For each generated triplet, we first construct a candidate set of prompts. During prompt-variation generation, we also prompt an LLM to identify the aspects of the images that are intended to change. If the images were fully described by the input text prompts, this would be sufficient. However, as the mapping between prompts and images is not one-to-one, images may vary from the prompt, or show additional unspecified properties. As such, we pass the triplet and the candidate list to a VLM for refinement, removing unrelated ones and adding visually-varying factors that are not explicit in the prompts (e.g., pose or object size). The resulting aspect list is intentionally over-complete, and it is not guaranteed to be aligned with how humans describe (or attend to) differences in the triplet. We therefore treat these as proposals and prune. For each triplet, we ask 5 annotators for judgments. We provide an additional “can’t tell” option, and if marked by 3 or more users, we remove the attribute from the list. From the remaining triplets we remove the “can’t tell” votes and normalize to get probability distribution 𝐲 = ( y 1 , y 2 , y 3 ) ∈ Δ 3 \mathbf{y}=(y_{1},y_{2},y_{3})\in\Delta^{3} . We also ask for overall similarity, recorded under the “overall” condition. However, we find a substantial gap between current VLMs’ zero-shot judgments and human perceptual choices (Section 5 ), motivating task-specific fine-tuning. As shown in Figure 3 (right), we explore three architectures that differ in how early the two images interact in the network, ranging from no interaction (late fusion) to full joint attention (early fusion). All three are trained end-to-end with our loss (Equation 2 ). Late fusion (embeddings). We repurpose the VLM as a text-guided embedding model, following recent work on instruction-tuned VLM retrievers [ 67 , 68 ] . We provide more qualitative results in Appendix B.1 . 6 Discussion, Broader Impacts, and Limitations Beyond using our metric as a human-grained, aspect-conditioned judge, it can serve as a feedback signal to improve them, as recent work has leveraged VLM feedback to train image editing [ 74 , 75 ] and generation [ 37 , 76 ] models. Our method can also aid in interpretability systems that automatically discover and characterize neural features [ 77 , 78 ] . Our metric offers human-aligned measurements to assess which fine-grained visual properties the discovered features encode. As generative and perceptual vision systems see broader deployment, interpretability becomes essential for public oversight, accountability, and informed regulation. Our VLM-based metric is substantially more expensive to compute than LPIPS or DreamSim. Also, our current embedding-based retrieval requires separate feature encoding and indexing for each aspect condition. In addition, our annotator pool is not representative of all viewers; perception varies across people, and our metric inherits that bias. Our method is also limited by training data diversity. We source prompts from FLUX-Reason-6M [ 66 ] , which has more aesthetically curated images. Our aspect proposals are VLM-generated, and we can systematically miss aspects that VLMs cannot capture. Since our triplets often share similar semantic content, our learned metric is not fully disentangled from the original content (e.g., sunny beach images will have higher weather similarity scores on other similar sunny beach images than sunny forest images). Data-related issues could be addressed with more diverse image sources and human-annotated aspects in future work. That said, as VLMs continue to improve, our pipeline naturally benefits — and we view our human perceptual data as a complementary signal toward building more human-aligned models, offering a new angle for collecting fine-grained human perceptual judgments.
